name: Great Market Hall
description: The Great Market Hall at Fővám tér is Budapest's largest indoor market: a steel-and-brick hall opened in 1897 with a colourful tiled roof, selling produce, paprika and local food across three floors. It stands at the Pest end of Liberty Bridge.

children.text: The Great Market Hall (Nagyvásárcsarnok) was designed and built by Samu Pecz and opened with a ceremony on 15 February 1897. It stands at Fővám tér, at the end of Váci utca on the Pest side of the Liberty Bridge. The steel structure covers around 10,000 square metres, behind a brick facade with a neo-Gothic entrance gate, and the roof is covered in colourful Zsolnay tiles from Pécs.

Inside, the stalls are spread over three floors. On the ground floor you find fresh produce, meat, pastries, sweets, spices and spirits, together with the food souvenirs visitors take home: paprika, Tokaji wine, Túró Rudi, kolbász sausage and salami. The upper level has eateries and souvenir stalls, and the basement holds fishmongers, pickled-vegetable stalls and some specialist butchers.

The hall was heavily damaged in World War II and then deteriorated. A thorough renovation began in 1991 when the hall was closed; Hungarian sources give 1994 for the end of the reconstruction, while English Wikipedia says the market reopened in 1997. In 1999 it received the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence.
It works both as a place for local shoppers and as a sightseeing stop. Go earlier in the day for the fresh produce and a calmer atmosphere; the upper-floor food stalls are popular at lunchtime.
Good to know
Opening days and hours vary: check the current times before you go.
Prices differ from stall to stall, especially for food souvenirs: compare before you buy.
The Liberty Bridge, Váci utca and the Gellért Thermal Bath are close by.

historyIntro: Budapest's Great Market Hall is more than a souvenir stop: it represents the modernisation of the city's everyday food trade at the end of the nineteenth century.

historySections.heading: A grand new home for market life

children.text: The hall was created during the period when Budapest was expanding its infrastructure and public buildings. Its vast iron-supported interior and striking roof turned the shopping of food into part of the city's architectural story.
Today, visitors encounter market stalls and Hungarian products under one of the city's distinctive historic interiors. Trading patterns vary, so the experience can differ by day.

name: Margaret Island Water Tower
description: A reinforced-concrete tower in the middle of Margaret Island, completed in 1911 to supply the island with water and to serve as a lookout. Designed by engineer Szilárd Zielinski with architect Rezső Vilmos Ray, it is 57 metres high and today also hosts exhibitions and festival events.

children.text: The Margaret Island Water Tower stands in the central part of the island, next to the open-air stage. It was completed in 1911 to secure the island's growing water supply and was designed from the start to work both as a water tower and as a lookout. The engineering was entrusted to Dr. Szilárd Zielinski, a professor at the Technical University and a European pioneer of reinforced concrete who introduced the material to Hungary; he worked with the architect and designer Rezső Vilmos Ray. The official tower site calls their collaboration a major technological innovation in modern Hungarian architecture.

The official technical data give a height of 57 metres, a water tank 13 metres in diameter with a capacity of 600 cubic metres, and main columns with a free height of 13.2 metres. A concrete staircase 24 metres high and an iron staircase 20 metres high add up to 153 steps. A Hungarian tourism page names the dome hall, with its floor 27 metres up, as the highest publicly accessible level, and a Budapest article describes an Art Nouveau spiral staircase leading to a viewing room with eight balconies and views of the city, the Danube bridges and the Buda hills.

The tower was declared a monument of townscape significance in 1977. It has been operated by the island's open-air theatre since 2011, and since 2012 it has served as a lookout tower, a visual art exhibition space and a venue for the Budapest Summer Festival. The Grand Stage and the Water Tower were rebuilt in two phases, in 2013 and 2014, with funding from the Government of Hungary and the Municipality of Budapest.

The tower makes sense against the island around it. Margaret Island is about 2.5 kilometres long and 500 metres wide and lies in the Danube between Margaret Bridge and Árpád Bridge. It takes its name from Princess Margaret, daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent there in the 13th century, and Wikipedia notes that its present form came from joining three islands at the end of the 19th century. Other sights include the Centenary Memorial, the Musical Fountain, the Japanese Garden and the Palatinus bath.
Good to know
Check the official tower site for current opening times, tickets and any closures on performance days or holidays; access to the lookout varies.
The tower stands beside the Margaret Island open-air stage in the middle of the island, so it combines easily with a walk through the parkland.
Car access to the island has been restricted since the 1980s, so plan to arrive on foot, by bicycle or by public transport.

historyIntro: The Water Tower stands as a striking piece of early modern engineering on Margaret Island, now linking industry, art and the island's leisure culture.

historySections.heading: A functional landmark above the trees

children.text: Built to supply water for the island, the tall tower became one of its most recognisable structures. Its architecture reflects a time when utility buildings could also be ambitious elements of the city skyline.

Instead of remaining only an infrastructure site, the tower has been used for exhibitions and views, connected to the island's open-air theatre and cultural programmes. Access to these functions varies with events.

name: Liszt Ferenc Academy of Music
description: A concert hall and music academy in an Art Nouveau building by Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl, completed in 1907 at Liszt Ferenc Square. Zsolnay ceramics, Miksa Róth stained glass and a Liszt statue by Alajos Stróbl mark it, and a restoration won a Europa Nostra Grand Prix in 2015.

children.text: The Liszt Ferenc Academy of Music, known in Hungarian as the Zeneakadémia, is both a working music university and a concert venue. It was founded on 14 November 1875 by Franz Liszt in his own home, and Wikipedia notes that it was named after him only in 1925. Its first purpose-built home, a three-storey neo-Renaissance building by Adolf Láng on today's Andrássy Avenue, served from 1877 to 1879 according to Wikipedia and now houses the Ferenc Liszt Memorial and Research Centre.

The Academy outgrew that building, and in 1907 it moved into its current home at the corner of Király Street and Liszt Ferenc Square. This Art Nouveau building was designed by Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl at the request of Baron Gyula Wlassics, then Minister of Culture. A statue of Liszt by Alajos Stróbl dominates the facade. Inside there are frescoes, Zsolnay ceramics and statues of Béla Bartók and Frédéric Chopin, and Miksa Róth made the original stained glass windows. Motifs related to Apollo and Dionysus appear throughout.

The Great Hall keeps some of its original character: its curtains in front of the glass windows are the originals from 1907, and the seat upholstery uses the same velvet. A Visit Hungary article says the armrests in the banquet hall are lower than expected so listeners can relax, and that the best acoustic seats are in the fifth row.

The European Heritage Awards entry says the concert halls and interiors were heavily altered in the 1950s. After more than a century of use, the building's systems were outdated, so the restoration reinforced the structure, installed modern mechanical, electrical and air conditioning systems and used archive photographs and on-site research to restore original materials, textures and colours. The project received the Grand Prix of the European Heritage Awards and Europa Nostra Awards in 2015.

Many well-known musicians taught at the Academy, including Liszt, Béla Bartók, Zoltán Kodály, Ernő Dohnányi, Jenő Hubay, Leo Weiner and György Kurtág, according to Wikipedia's selection. The Academy also keeps the Liszt Collection of books and manuscripts that Liszt left on his death, and its Franz Liszt Museum shows three restored rooms from his home.
Good to know
Check the Academy's official site for the concert calendar, guided visits and tickets, since the building is also a working university.
The facade and the Liszt statue can be seen from the street at the corner of Király Street and Liszt Ferenc Square.
The Liszt Memorial and Research Centre in the Academy's first building is a separate site on Andrássy Avenue, so check its own page before planning to visit both.

historyIntro: The Liszt Academy links the career of one of Hungary's most celebrated composers with the country's concert and music-training traditions.

children.text: Franz Liszt helped establish the music academy tradition in Budapest during the nineteenth century. The institution developed into an internationally known conservatory and concert centre, bringing education and public performance together.

The historic academy building serves both students and visiting audiences. Its concert halls, decorative surfaces and performance programme make it a living part of Budapest's musical life, not merely a memorial to a single composer.

name: Pesti Vigadó
description: A Romantic-style cultural centre on the Pest embankment, designed by Frigyes Feszl and opened in 1865 on the site of an older dance hall. Liszt, Brahms and Dvořák performed there, and a restoration reopened the building in 2014 with a Danube-facing panorama terrace.

children.text: The Pesti Vigadó is a cultural centre on the Danube embankment in Pest, designed by Frigyes Feszl, who was commissioned in 1859. It was built on the site of the Redoute, a hall designed by Mihály Pollack, the architect of the Hungarian National Museum. The Redoute was completed in 1832 and opened to the public in 1833, and before 1848 it was Pest's only concert hall. It was destroyed in May 1849 by Heinrich Hentzi, commander of the Austrian-occupied Buda Castle, during the siege of Buda.

Construction of the new building began in 1860, and it opened with a grand ball on 15 January 1865. It is considered a symbol of Hungarian Romantic architecture, though Hungary Today notes it was not well received by the public or professionals at the time. Feszl wanted mosaics for the interior walls but the Pest City Council chose paintings, which made it the first public building in Pest decorated with frescoes. The hall was nicknamed Vigarda in mockery before the name Vigadó stuck.

Its history is closely tied to the country's public life. According to Hungary Today, Franz Liszt gave the first concert in the Redoute after the 1838 flood and played his Rákóczi March there for the first time, but other sources credit Ferenc Erkel with organising that charity concert and place Liszt's first visit to the Redoute in 1839, so the details are uncertain. On 11 July 1848 the first National Assembly delegates offered 200,000 recruits for the country's defence. A ball celebrated Franz Joseph I's coronation in 1867, and the unification of Pest, Buda and Óbuda into Budapest was celebrated in the building in 1873. Johann Strauss, Antonín Dvořák and the Budapest Philharmonic Orchestra made debuts here, and in 1881 Brahms was soloist in the premiere of his Piano Concerto in B-flat major.

The building was badly damaged in 1945 and listed as a historic monument in 1954. Reconstruction began in 1968, and the rebuilt hall opened to the public on 15 March 1980 according to the Vigadó's own history page; Hungary Today gives 12 March and mentions 660-seat and 200-seat halls. It closed in 2004, the Hungarian Academy of Arts acquired it in 2013, and it reopened on 14 March 2014 after restoration. A permanent exhibition on the building's history opened on 27 May 2017.

Today the Vigadó presents concerts, theatre, contemporary art and other exhibitions. Visit Hungary lists the Vigadó Galéria with five exhibition halls, a Banquet Hall, the Sinkovits Imre Chamber Theatre and a Panorama Terrace that overlooks the Danube, Buda Castle and the Citadella.
Good to know
Check the Vigadó's official site for the current programme, exhibitions, tours and tickets, as individual venues inside the building have separate schedules.
The building stands on the Pest Danube embankment, so it fits naturally into a riverside walk.
Its panorama terrace faces the river, Buda Castle and Gellért Hill's Citadella, but confirm access on the official page.

historyIntro: Pesti Vigadó has been part of Budapest's cultural riverfront since the nineteenth century, linking architecture with concerts, meetings and celebrations.

historySections.heading: A grand gathering place by the river

children.text: The Vigadó developed as a ceremonial and performance venue in the heart of Pest, reflecting the city's growing appetite for major cultural spaces. Its façade and richly decorated rooms were created for public occasions.

The building was badly damaged during the Second World War and remained under reconstruction for decades. It reopened in 1980, and the restored venue has since hosted music, art and other cultural programmes.
